title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes, no, thank you and sorry, and choose the right word for 'you'.
intro:
Punjabi greetings depend a little on who you are talking to. In Indian Punjab, **ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ** is the everyday greeting used with almost everyone; Hindus may say **ਨਮਸਤੇ**, and in Pakistan and among Muslims **ਅੱਸਲਾਮ ਅਲੈਕੁਮ** is normal. The magic word in Punjabi politeness is **ਜੀ** (*jī*): add it to greetings, names and answers and you instantly sound respectful.

Remember the tones as you go: ਧੰਨਵਾਦ (*tànnvād*) starts low, ਨਹੀਂ (*nahī̀ṃ*) has a low tone on its stressed second syllable.

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Punjabi sentences normally put the **verb at the end**: subject, then object or other information, then the verb. 'I drink tea' is literally 'I tea drink'. Little words like ਹੈ (*is*) and ਹਾਂ (*am*) come last too.

Question words don't move to the front as in English: they sit where the answer would go, usually just before the verb. A yes/no question is the same as a statement with rising intonation; you can add ਕੀ at the start to make it explicit.

**Negation**: put ਨਹੀਂ right before the verb (and the ਹੈ/ਹਾਂ is often dropped).

examples.en: I drink tea. (I tea drinking am — man speaking)
What do you drink? (you what drink?)

grammar.title: Three ways to say 'you': ਤੂੰ, ਤੁਸੀਂ, ਆਪ
grammar.body:
**ਤੂੰ** (*tūṃ*) is intimate: for small children, very close friends of your own age, younger siblings — and God in prayer. Using it with a stranger or an elder is rude.

**ਤੁਸੀਂ** (*tusīṃ*) is the normal polite form for any adult, and also the plural 'you (all)'. Its verb ending is -ਓ / ਹੋ. This is the form to use as a learner.

**ਆਪ** (*āp*) is very formal: speeches, announcements, letters, or showing great deference. In everyday speech it is less common than in Hindi.

To be extra respectful, add **ਜੀ**: ਹਾਂ ਜੀ 'yes', ਨਹੀਂ ਜੀ 'no', ਗਿੱਲ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, ਮਾਤਾ ਜੀ. Verbs agree with the pronoun: ਤੂੰ … ਹੈਂ, ਤੁਸੀਂ … ਹੋ.

examples.en: How are you? (to a close friend or child)

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Simran meets her neighbour Mr Gill in the street in the morning.

lines.speaker: Mr Gill
lines.native: ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ ਬੇਟਾ! ਕੀ ਹਾਲ ਹੈ?
lines.roman: sat srī akāl beṭā! kī hāl hai?

lines.speaker: Simran
lines.native: ਮੈਂ ਠੀਕ ਹਾਂ ਜੀ। ਤੁਸੀਂ ਸੁਣਾਓ?
lines.roman: maiṃ ṭhīk hāṃ jī. tusīṃ suṇāo?

lines.speaker: Mr Gill
lines.native: ਵਧੀਆ, ਰੱਬ ਦਾ ਸ਼ੁਕਰ ਹੈ। ਚਾਹ ਪੀਓਗੇ?
lines.roman: vadī̀ā, rabb dā shukar hai. chā́ pīoge?
lines.en: Great, thank God. Will you have some tea?

culture: Greetings in Punjab often signal community, but people happily use each other's greetings: a Muslim from Lahore and a Sikh from Amritsar may greet each other with ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ and ਅੱਸਲਾਮ ਅਲੈਕੁਮ in turn. Young people often just say 'hi' or 'hello' in English. Older people are addressed with kinship terms rather than names — ਅੰਕਲ ਜੀ, ਆਂਟੀ ਜੀ, ਭਾਜੀ (brother), ਭੈਣ ਜੀ (sister) — even if they are strangers. Folding your hands, or a light hand on the heart, accompanies a respectful greeting; touching the feet of elders shows great respect within families.

tip.title: The verb goes last
tip.body:
- Punjabi puts the verb at the **end**: ਮੈਂ ਠੀਕ ਹਾਂ is literally 'I fine am'.
- **ਹਾਂ** = am (with ਮੈਂ), **ਹੋ** = are (with ਤੁਸੀਂ), **ਹੈ** = is.
- Question words like **ਕਿਵੇਂ** 'how' and **ਕੀ** 'what' sit just before the verb: ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿਵੇਂ ਹੋ?

sentences.native: ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ ਜੀ, ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿਵੇਂ ਹੋ?
sentences.roman: sat srī akāl jī, tusīṃ kiveṃ ho?
maiṃ ṭhīk hāṃ, tusīṃ kiveṃ ho?

tip.title: ਜੀ, ਨਹੀਂ and saying thanks
tip.body:
- Add **ਜੀ** to sound polite: ਹਾਂ ਜੀ 'yes', ਨਹੀਂ ਜੀ 'no'. (ਹਾਂ means both 'yes' and 'am'.)
- **ਨਹੀਂ** 'not' goes just before the verb, and ਹਾਂ/ਹੈ is often dropped: ਮੈਂ ਠੀਕ ਨਹੀਂ.
- Thanks: **ਧੰਨਵਾਦ** (standard), **ਸ਼ੁਕਰੀਆ** (casual), **ਤੁਹਾਡੀ ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ** (warm). The reply: ਕੋਈ ਗੱਲ ਨਹੀਂ.

sentences.en: Thank you, that's kind of you.

sentences.native: ਹਾਂ ਜੀ, ਰੱਬ ਦਾ ਸ਼ੁਕਰ ਹੈ।
sentences.roman: hāṃ jī, rabb dā shukar hai.

tip.title: Polite requests end in -ਓ
tip.body:
- To ask someone politely, use the **-ਓ** form of the verb: **ਸੁਣੋ** 'listen', **ਬੋਲੋ** 'speak', **ਦੱਸੋ** 'tell'. Add **ਜੀ** to soften it.
- **ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ** is both 'sorry' and 'excuse me'; **ਸੁਣੋ ਜੀ** gets someone's attention.
- ਕਿਰਪਾ ਕਰਕੇ 'please' is formal; in speech ਜੀ usually does the job.

sentences.en: Excuse me, sorry to bother you.

sentences.native: ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ, ਮੈਨੂੰ ਸਮਝ ਨਹੀਂ ਆਈ।
sentences.roman: māf karnā, mainūṃ samáj nahī̀ṃ āī.

sentences.native: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਸਮਝ ਨਹੀਂ ਆਈ, ਦੁਬਾਰਾ ਬੋਲੋ ਜੀ।
sentences.roman: mainūṃ samáj nahī̀ṃ āī, dubārā bolo jī.
sentences.en: I didn't understand, please say it again.

sentences.native: ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ ਜੀ, ਤੁਸੀਂ ਠੀਕ ਹੋ?
sentences.roman: māf karnā jī, tusīṃ ṭhīk ho?

tip.title: Three ways to say 'you'
tip.body:
- **ਤੁਸੀਂ** (polite) → verb **ਹੋ**: any adult, strangers, shopkeepers. When unsure, use ਤੁਸੀਂ.
- **ਤੂੰ** (intimate) → verb **ਹੈਂ**: children and very close friends only.
- **ਆਪ** is very formal (speeches, letters).
- Call a man **ਭਾਜੀ** 'brother', an older man **ਅੰਕਲ ਜੀ**.

sentences.en: I'm fine, and you? (to a close friend)

tip.title: Closing a conversation
tip.body:
- **ਚੰਗਾ ਜੀ** 'OK then' signals you're about to leave.
- Then a goodbye: **ਰੱਬ ਰਾਖਾ** (everyone), **ਖ਼ੁਦਾ ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼** (Muslim usage), or simply **ਸਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅਕਾਲ** again.
- **ਫਿਰ ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ** 'we'll meet again' = see you.
